headline: Summer is over. Give your roof a once-over.
title: Fall Roof Check After Summer Heat | Integrity Roofing
desc: October roof tips for Phoenix Valley homeowners: a safe fall check after summer heat and monsoon storms, plus a DIY tip, quick checklist and FAQs.
h1: October 2026: Your fall roof check after a long Phoenix summer
lead: The heat is finally easing and monsoon season ended September 30. October is a comfortable month to look at what summer did to your roof, before winter rain arrives.
answer: In October, look over your roof from the ground and from inside your home for signs of summer wear: cracked or slipped tiles, dried-out sealant, blistered coatings and new ceiling stains. Clear gutters and scuppers, and get any problems repaired before winter rains start, usually in December.

sections.h2: What a Phoenix summer does to your roof
sections.body:
Every summer puts your roof through a stress test. For months, the sun beats down on the surface, and roof materials get far hotter than the air around them. Then the temperature drops at night, and everything shrinks back. That daily cycle of expanding and contracting slowly loosens fasteners, opens small gaps and wears on seams.

Ultraviolet light does its own damage. It dries out sealants around vents and skylights, cracks the rubber boots that wrap plumbing pipes, and breaks down the top layer of coatings on flat and foam roofs. On asphalt shingles, heat and UV loosen the protective granules, which you may notice collecting at the bottom of downspouts.

Then come the monsoon storms. Strong gusts can lift or shift tiles, blow debris into valleys, and push rain sideways into spots that normally stay dry. Some of that damage is obvious. Much of it hides until the next steady rain finds the weak spot.

sections.h2: Why October is the right time to look
sections.body:
October gives you a window. Temperatures are pleasant again, monsoon storms are behind us, and winter rain is still weeks away. That makes it the best time of year to spot small problems and get them handled while they are still small.

A cracked tile or a split pipe boot is usually a modest repair. Left alone through a few winter storms, the same problem can soak the underlayment, stain drywall and reach insulation. Fixing it in fall means you are not scrambling during the first rainy week of the year, when many homeowners discover leaks at the same time.

If you are not sure what you are looking at, a professional roof inspection gives you a clear picture of your roof's condition and what, if anything, needs attention.

sections.h2: DIY tip of the month: do a binocular walk-around
sections.body:
You can learn a lot about your roof without ever leaving the ground. Grab a pair of binoculars and your phone, and walk slowly around the whole house in the morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and shadows show up broken edges.

Look along each roof slope for tiles that sit higher or lower than their neighbors, missing pieces, and dark gaps. Check ridges and hips for mortar or caps that look loose. Look at vents, pipes and the edges where the roof meets a wall. Take photos of anything that seems off so you can compare later. Please don't climb onto the roof, and never walk on tile. Tiles crack easily underfoot, and a fall from any roof is serious.
Spend 30 minutes on these this month:
bullets: Walk around the house with binoculars and photograph any cracked, slipped or missing tiles or shingles.
Look for granules or tile chips collecting at downspouts and along the drip line.
Clear leaves and debris from gutters, downspouts and flat-roof scuppers using a tool you can operate from the ground.
Check ceilings, closets and the tops of walls for new water stains or bubbled paint.
Look at the sides of the house under roof edges for streaks that might signal overflow.
Trim back branches that touch or hang over the roof (hire help for tall trees).
Make a short list of concerns so you have it ready if you call for an inspection.

sections.body:
On a summer afternoon, a roof surface in direct sun can be dramatically hotter than the air temperature, especially if the material is dark. That is why heat is one of the biggest causes of long-term roof wear in the desert, even more than rain.

Phoenix also has two rainy seasons, not one: the summer monsoon and the winter storm season. A fall check sits right between them, which makes it one of the most useful habits a Valley homeowner can build.

Thanks for reading The Integrity Roofing Monthly. If your walk-around turned up anything that worries you, give us a call at 602-548-3770, Monday to Friday, 7 am to 5 pm. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours. Next month: hanging holiday lights without damaging your roof.

faqs: Is October a good time to schedule roof repairs in Phoenix?
Yes. The weather is mild, monsoon season is over and winter rains have not started yet. Repairs made in fall protect your home before the steady storms of December and January arrive.
How can I tell if summer heat damaged my roof?

From the ground, look for cracked or shifted tiles, curling or bare shingles, and blistered or peeling coating on flat roofs. Inside, look for ceiling stains. Many heat-related problems, like dried-out sealant, are only visible up close, which is where a professional inspection helps.
Should I worry about granules in my gutters?

A few granules are normal on any asphalt shingle roof. Large amounts, or bare patches visible on the shingles, can mean the roof is aging and losing its UV protection. It is worth having it looked at.
Can monsoon damage show up weeks later?
It can. Wind can loosen a tile or open a seam without causing an immediate leak. The problem often shows up during the next long, steady rain, which in the Valley is usually a winter storm.
Is it safe for me to get on my roof to check it?

We recommend staying off the roof. Tile cracks easily when walked on, roof surfaces can be slippery or hot, and falls cause serious injuries. Use binoculars from the ground and leave the up-close work to a licensed roofer.

headline: Deck the halls, not the tiles
title: Hang Holiday Lights Without Roof Damage | Integrity Roofing
desc: November roof tips: how to hang holiday lights on a Phoenix tile or shingle roof using clips instead of nails or staples, plus a safety checklist and FAQs.
h1: November 2026: Hang holiday lights without damaging your roof
lead: Holiday lights make a house glow, but nails, staples and careless climbing can leave you with cracked tiles and leaks long after the decorations come down. Here is how to light up your home and keep your roof intact.
answer: Hang holiday lights with plastic clips designed for gutters, shingles or roof edges, never nails, screws or staples, which create holes that let water in. Avoid walking on tile roofs, work from a properly placed ladder, and keep lights along the eaves, fascia and gutters rather than across the roof surface.

sections.h2: Why nails and staples are a bad idea
sections.body:
Every hole you put in a roof is a potential leak. A staple through a shingle or a nail into the fascia right at the drip edge may look harmless, but it opens a path for water. In a dry November, you won't notice. When the winter storms come in December and January, water can follow that hole into the roof deck.

Tile roofs add another risk. Concrete and clay tiles are strong when they sit in place, but they crack under concentrated weight. A single step in the wrong spot can break a tile, and a broken tile exposes the underlayment beneath it to sun and rain. Many holiday-light repairs we hear about start with someone walking up a tile roof to string lights along the ridge.

Plastic light clips are inexpensive, easy to use and made for exactly this job. There are styles that hook onto gutter lips, slip under shingle edges without fasteners, or grip the edge of fascia boards. Most hardware stores carry them, and the packaging will tell you which roof type each one fits.

For tile roofs, keep lights at the eaves and gutters. Clips that attach to the gutter or fascia let you outline the roofline from a ladder without touching the tiles. If you love the look of lights along the ridge or across the roof, consider hiring a holiday lighting installer who uses fastener-free methods, or swap in ground-level displays like lit trees, stakes and projectors.

Whatever you choose, use lights and extension cords rated for outdoor use, and plug them into a GFCI-protected outlet.

sections.h2: DIY tip of the month: plan and pre-clip on the ground
sections.body:
The less time you spend on a ladder, the safer you are. Before you climb, lay your light strands out on the driveway, test every strand, and attach the clips at even spacing while you are standing on solid ground. Then all you have to do on the ladder is hook each clip in place.

Set your ladder on firm, level ground, and use the 4-to-1 rule: for every 4 feet of height, the base should be 1 foot out from the wall. Have someone hold the ladder, keep three points of contact, and move the ladder often rather than leaning out to reach. Stay off the roof itself.
Before the lights go up:
bullets: Buy clips made for your roof edge: gutter, shingle or fascia style.
Test every strand on the ground and replace any with cracked sockets or frayed wires.
Use outdoor-rated lights and cords, plugged into a GFCI outlet.
Check your ladder for loose rungs and set it on firm, level ground.
Keep lights on the eaves and gutters, not across tile surfaces.
Never use nails, screws or staples in the roof or fascia edge.
Pick a take-down date and plan to remove clips gently in January.

sections.body:
LED holiday lights use a small fraction of the electricity of old incandescent strands and run much cooler to the touch. That makes them easier on your power bill and less of a concern around dry leaves in gutters.

Ladder falls are one of the most common causes of home injuries around the holidays. Taking an extra minute to move the ladder instead of reaching is one of the simplest safety habits there is.

From all of us at Integrity Roofing, a family-owned company since 1993, happy holidays. If you find a cracked tile or a suspicious spot while decorating, call us at 602-548-3770, Monday to Friday, 7 am to 5 pm. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours. Next month: getting ready for winter rain.

faqs: Can I staple holiday lights to my shingles?
Please don't. Staples puncture the shingle and can let water reach the roof deck. Plastic shingle clips slide under the edge and hold lights securely without any holes.
Is it safe to walk on my tile roof to hang lights?
No. Concrete and clay tiles can crack under a person's weight, and broken tiles can lead to leaks. They can also be slippery. Hang lights from a ladder at the eaves and gutters instead.
What kind of clips work on a tile roof?
Gutter clips and fascia clips are the safest choices because they don't touch the tiles at all. Avoid clips that wedge between tiles, since they can lift or crack them.
How should I take holiday lights down?
Unhook clips one at a time from a ladder rather than pulling the whole strand. Yanking can bend gutters, pull clips through brittle edges or knock tiles loose.
What if I notice roof damage while decorating?
Take a photo from where you are, stay off the roof and give us a call. A cracked tile or lifted shingle is usually a simple repair if it is handled before winter rain.

headline: Winter rain finds what summer broke
title: Winter Rain and Roof Leaks in Phoenix | Integrity Roofing
desc: December roof tips for Phoenix homeowners: how winter rains expose leaks, the warning signs to watch for inside, and safe steps to take if water gets in.
h1: December 2026: Winter rains and how to catch roof leaks early
lead: Winter storms in the Valley are usually gentler than monsoon storms, but they last longer. A slow, steady rain is very good at finding small weak spots in a roof.
answer: December and January rains are long and steady, so they often reveal leaks that started as summer heat or monsoon damage. Watch ceilings, closets and the attic for stains or damp spots, keep gutters and drains clear, and call a roofer as soon as you see signs of water so a small leak doesn't become a big repair.

sections.body:
Monsoon storms hit hard and fast. Winter storms are different. They arrive from the Pacific and can bring hours of light to moderate rain, sometimes for a day or more. That slow soaking gives water time to work its way under a cracked tile, through a split pipe boot or around a gap in flashing.

On tile roofs, the tile sheds most of the water, but the underlayment beneath it is the real waterproof layer. If that underlayment is old, brittle or torn, a long rain is when you find out. On flat and foam roofs, low spots that hold water after a storm, called ponding, can slowly push moisture through worn coatings.

Cold nights add one more factor. When the roof cools, condensation can collect in the attic, and damp insulation can look like a leak even when the roof is sound. A roofer can help you tell the difference.

sections.h2: Signs of a leak to watch for
sections.body:
Most leaks show up inside before you see anything outside. After the first few rains of the season, take a walk through your home and look up. Check ceilings in every room, especially near exterior walls, around light fixtures and under bathroom vent fans.

Look for yellow or brown rings, bubbling or peeling paint, sagging drywall, or a musty smell that wasn't there before. Water travels along rafters and pipes, so the spot you see may be several feet from the actual opening in the roof. Note where and when you see it. That information helps a roofer find the source quickly.

If you spot a stain, a professional roof repair visit is usually the fastest route to stopping it.

sections.h2: DIY tip of the month: set up a leak response kit
sections.body:
A small kit kept in a closet makes a surprise leak much less stressful. Gather a couple of buckets, old towels, a plastic drop cloth, a flashlight, painter's tape and a phone ready to take photos.

If water starts dripping, move furniture and electronics away, put down plastic and a bucket, and photograph the spot. If a ceiling bulges with water, keep people out from under it, and if there is any chance water is near light fixtures or wiring, turn off power to that area at the breaker. Do not go up on the roof in the rain to look for the problem. Wet tile and shingles are extremely slippery. Wait for dry weather and call a roofer.
Before and during the rainy weeks:
bullets: Clear gutters, downspouts and scuppers before the first big storm.
Make sure downspouts drain away from the foundation.
After each rain, walk through the house and check ceilings and closet corners.
Peek into the attic with a flashlight from the access hatch and look for damp spots or stained wood.
Take dated photos of any stains so you can tell if they grow.
Keep your leak response kit somewhere easy to reach.
Call for repairs as soon as you see water, not after the season ends.

sections.body:
Phoenix has two distinct rainy seasons. The summer monsoon brings short, intense thunderstorms, while winter brings longer storms from Pacific weather systems. The Valley averages only about 7 inches of rain a year, which is one reason small roof problems can go unnoticed for months.

On a tile roof, the tiles are mainly there to protect the underlayment from sun and to shed the bulk of the water. The underlayment underneath does the real waterproofing work.

We hope your holidays are warm and dry. If you see a stain or drip this winter, call us at 602-548-3770, Monday to Friday, 7 am to 5 pm. We are closed weekends, so if we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours. Next month: a simple roof plan for the new year.

faqs: Why does my roof only leak in winter?

Winter storms bring long, steady rain that gives water time to find small openings. Monsoon storms are intense but short. A leak that only appears in winter often points to aging underlayment, flashing gaps or cracked tiles.
Is a ceiling stain always a roof leak?
Not always. Plumbing leaks, AC condensate lines and attic condensation can cause stains too. If the stain appears or grows after rain, the roof is the most likely cause, and a roofer can confirm it.
Should I put a tarp on my roof myself?
We don't recommend it. Climbing onto a wet roof is dangerous, and walking on tile can crack more tiles. Contain the water inside, take photos and call a roofer when the weather allows.
How fast should a roof leak be repaired?

As soon as you can. Water that keeps getting in can soak insulation, damage drywall and lead to mold or wood rot. A quick repair is almost always less costly than repairing the damage a long-running leak leaves behind.
Can winter rain damage a foam or flat roof?

Yes, especially where water ponds after a storm. Standing water stresses worn coatings and can find its way through small cracks. Keeping drains and scuppers clear and maintaining the coating helps a lot.

headline: A roof plan for the new year
title: New Year Roof Plan and Attic Check | Integrity Roofing
desc: January roof tips for Phoenix homeowners: build a simple year-round roof plan, do a safe attic check, and know what to look for before spring and monsoon.
h1: January 2027: Start the year with a roof plan and an attic check
lead: New year, fresh list. A few minutes of planning now can help you catch roof problems early, budget for what's ahead and avoid surprises when monsoon season arrives.
answer: Start the year by writing down your roof's age, type and repair history, then plan an inspection in spring before monsoon season begins June 15. A careful attic check in cool January weather can reveal leaks, daylight gaps, pest activity and ventilation problems that you can't see from the outside.

sections.body:
You don't need a spreadsheet. A single page, or a note on your phone, is enough. Start with the basics: what kind of roof you have (tile, shingle, foam or flat), roughly when it was installed, and any repairs you know about. If you bought the home recently, your inspection report or seller disclosures may have these details.

Next, map the year. Winter is for watching for leaks. Spring, especially March and April, is the best time for an inspection and repairs. May is for final pre-monsoon prep. Summer is for storm watching and after-storm checks. Fall is for looking at what summer did. Put two or three reminders on your calendar now, and you won't have to think about it again until they pop up.

If your roof is getting older, the plan is also a good time to learn what's ahead. Our Roofing Cost Guide explains what affects cost, though every roof is different.

sections.h2: Why January is a good month for the attic
sections.body:
The attic is the one place you can see the underside of your roof, and January is the most comfortable month to look. In summer, Valley attics get dangerously hot. In winter, you can take your time.

The attic also tells you things the outside can't. Water stains on the roof deck, damp insulation, daylight where there shouldn't be any, and droppings from birds or roof rats all show up here first. After the December rains, any active leak is likely to have left a mark.

sections.h2: DIY tip of the month: a safe attic check
sections.body:
Pick a dry, cool day and bring a bright flashlight, a dust mask, gloves and your phone. Use a sturdy ladder to reach the hatch, and look from the opening first. If you go further in, step only on the ceiling joists or on a walkway or boards. Stepping between joists can put your foot through the ceiling.

Shine your light along the underside of the roof deck and rafters. Look for dark stains, water rings, damp or matted insulation, and rusty nail tips. Turn your flashlight off for a moment and look for pinpoints of daylight. Check that vents are not blocked by insulation. Take photos of anything unusual. Watch your head on nails coming through the deck, and stay away from wiring.
Your January roof to-do list:
bullets: Write down your roof type, approximate age and repair history.
Add calendar reminders for a March or April inspection and a May pre-monsoon check.
Do a cool-weather attic check for stains, damp insulation, daylight and pests.
Gently remove holiday light clips from gutters and fascia.
Look over ceilings after each winter rain.
Save photos and repair receipts in one folder.
Check that the contractors you hire hold a current Arizona ROC license.

sections.body:
The Arizona Registrar of Contractors lets homeowners look up a contractor's license status online, along with any complaint history. It's a smart step before hiring anyone to work on your home. Our license is ROC #096629.

Insulation is rated by R-value, a measure of how well it resists heat flow. A higher number means better resistance, which matters a great deal in a desert attic that bakes all summer.

Happy new year from our family-owned team. If your attic check turned up stains or anything else that concerns you, call 602-548-3770, Monday to Friday, 7 am to 5 pm. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours. Next month: what tile underlayment is and why it matters.

faqs: How often should a Phoenix roof be inspected?
A good habit is once a year, ideally in spring before monsoon season, and again after any major storm. Older roofs and tile roofs with aging underlayment benefit from closer attention.
What does a water stain in the attic mean?

A dark ring or stain on the roof deck or rafters usually means water has gotten past the roof covering at some point. If the wood is damp or soft, the leak is likely active and should be repaired soon.
Is it normal to see daylight in my attic?
Light coming through vents is normal. Pinpoints of daylight through the roof deck itself are not. They can mean gaps, missing material or damage that may let water in.
How do I find out how old my roof is?
Check your home purchase paperwork, inspection report or permit records, or ask previous owners if you can. A roofer can also estimate age based on materials and condition.
What should I do if I see signs of roof rats or birds in the attic?

Take photos and avoid touching droppings without gloves and a mask. Pests often get in through gaps at roof edges or under tiles. A pest professional can handle the animals, and a roofer can close the openings.

headline: The layer under your tile
title: Tile Roof Underlayment Basics in Phoenix | Integrity Roofing
desc: February roof tips: why tile underlayment is the real waterproof layer, how Phoenix heat ages it, warning signs, and what a re-felt or lift and relay means.
h1: February 2027: Get to know the underlayment under your tile roof
lead: Tile roofs are famous for lasting a long time, but the tiles are only half the story. Underneath them is a layer most homeowners never see, and it does most of the waterproofing work.
answer: On a tile roof, the underlayment beneath the tiles is the main waterproof barrier, and in Phoenix heat it usually wears out long before the tiles do. If your tile roof is 20 years old or more, or you're seeing leaks with no broken tiles, have the underlayment checked. Replacing it, often called a re-felt or lift and relay, lets you reuse good tiles.

sections.body:
Concrete and clay tiles shed most of the rain that hits your roof, and they shield what's under them from the sun. But tiles overlap loosely by design. Wind-driven rain and runoff get beneath them, especially during strong storms. The underlayment is the sheet material between the tiles and the roof deck that catches that water and channels it down and off the roof.

On many older Valley homes, underlayment is asphalt-saturated felt. Newer roofs may use synthetic underlayment. Either way, it's the layer that keeps water out of your attic when everything is working correctly.

The space under a tile gets extremely hot in summer. Over many years, that heat dries out felt underlayment, making it brittle. It can crack, tear, or wear through at spots where water flows most, such as valleys, around vents and near the eaves. Where a tile has cracked or slipped, the exposed underlayment gets direct sun, and it breaks down even faster.

That's why a tile roof can look perfectly fine from the street while the layer underneath is near the end of its life. Many tile roofs in the Valley reach the point where the underlayment needs replacing while the tiles themselves still have plenty of years left.

sections.h2: What a re-felt or lift and relay means
sections.body:
When underlayment is worn out, the usual fix is not a whole new roof. In a tile underlayment replacement, sometimes called a re-felt or lift and relay, the roofer carefully removes the tiles, replaces the underlayment and flashings as needed, and then reinstalls the good tiles, replacing any that are broken.

This approach saves the cost of new tile and keeps the look of your home the same. Every roof is different, so the right answer depends on the condition of the deck, tiles and underlayment. An inspection will tell you where yours stands.

sections.h2: DIY tip of the month: look for underlayment clues
sections.body:
You can gather clues safely without touching the roof. From the ground, use binoculars to look at the lowest row of tiles along the eaves. Sometimes you can see the edge of the underlayment there. If it looks frayed, crumbly or sun-bleached, make a note.

In the attic, on a cool day, look for stains on the roof deck under valleys and around vent pipes, the common spots where worn underlayment lets water through. Check gutters for small dark flakes of material after a rain. Please stay off the tiles. Walking on them can crack them, and cracked tiles speed up underlayment wear.
Tile roof owners, this one's for you:
bullets: Find out roughly when your roof or underlayment was installed.
From the ground, look for cracked or slipped tiles that expose underlayment.
Check the attic for stains under valleys and around pipes.
Note any leaks that happen without visible tile damage.
Look for dark flakes or debris in gutters after storms.
Keep a list of questions for your next inspection.
Plan underlayment work for spring or fall, when weather is mild.

sections.body:
Clay roof tiles have been used for thousands of years, from ancient China and Greece to the Mediterranean styles that influence many Arizona homes today. Concrete tile is much more recent, made from a mix of cement, sand and water.

Both types can outlast the underlayment beneath them by many years, which is why a re-felt is such a common project on Valley tile roofs.

If you'd like to know how your underlayment is holding up, call us at 602-548-3770, Monday to Friday, 7 am to 5 pm. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours. Next month: your spring inspection before monsoon season.

faqs: How long does tile roof underlayment last in Arizona?

It varies with the material, how well it was installed and how much sun reaches it. In the Valley's heat, felt underlayment often needs attention after about 20 years, sometimes sooner. An inspection is the only way to know for sure.
Can I replace underlayment without replacing my tiles?
Usually, yes. In a lift and relay, the tiles are removed, the underlayment is replaced, and the good tiles go back on. Broken tiles are replaced with matching ones where possible.
Why is my tile roof leaking if no tiles are broken?

The most common cause is worn underlayment. Tiles shed most of the water, but the underlayment beneath them keeps out what gets past. When it's brittle or torn, leaks can happen even with intact tiles.
Is synthetic underlayment better than felt?

Synthetic underlayment is lighter and tends to resist tearing, and many roofers use it today. The right choice depends on your roof and what the installer recommends for it. Ask about the options during your estimate.
When is the best time to replace underlayment?
Spring and fall are ideal in the Phoenix Valley, when temperatures are mild and storms are less likely. Doing it before monsoon season gives your roof a fresh barrier for the year's toughest weather.

headline: Spring check before the storms
title: Spring Roof Inspection Before Monsoon | Integrity Roofing
desc: March roof tips for Phoenix homeowners: why spring is the best time for a roof inspection before monsoon season, what inspectors check, and a safe DIY tip.
h1: March 2027: Schedule your spring roof inspection before monsoon season
lead: Spring in the Valley is short and lovely, and it's the best time of year to get your roof ready for the hard months ahead. Monsoon season starts June 15, and summer heat follows close behind.
answer: March and April are the ideal months for a roof inspection in the Phoenix Valley because the weather is mild and there's time to make repairs before monsoon season begins June 15. A good inspection checks tiles or shingles, flashing, underlayment, vents, drainage and the attic, so small problems can be fixed before storms test them.

sections.body:
Spring gives you comfortable temperatures, dry days and a clear runway before summer. Repairs that are easy to schedule in March can be harder to fit in once monsoon storms start and many homeowners call at once. Getting ahead of the rush means any repair happens on your timeline.

It also matters for the roof itself. Winter rains may have revealed slow leaks. Months of sun since last summer have aged sealants. Finding those issues now means the roof is ready when the first big storm rolls in.

A thorough roof inspection looks at the whole system, not just the surface. On tile roofs, that includes cracked, slipped or missing tiles, ridge and hip caps, and the condition of underlayment where it can be seen. On shingle roofs, it includes lifted or missing shingles, granule loss and nail pops. On flat and foam roofs, it covers the coating, seams, ponding areas and drains.

Inspectors also check the parts where leaks most often start: flashing around chimneys, walls and skylights, pipe boots, vents, valleys and roof edges. A look in the attic can show stains, ventilation issues and daylight gaps. Afterward, you should get a clear explanation of what's in good shape, what needs attention now and what to watch.

sections.h2: DIY tip of the month: clean the ground-level drainage path
sections.body:
Water that leaves your roof needs somewhere to go. Spring is a great time to make sure the path is clear from the gutter all the way to the yard. Standing on the ground, check that downspouts are attached firmly and that their outlets aren't buried in gravel, landscaping or debris.

Add or straighten splash blocks or extensions so water flows away from your foundation. For homes with flat roofs, look at the scupper outlets from below and note any staining on the walls beneath them, which can mean water is backing up. If gutters need cleaning, use a gutter tool with an extension pole from the ground, or hire help. Stay off the roof.
Spring prep, in order:
bullets: Schedule a roof inspection for March or April.
Gather your roof notes, photos and any questions for the inspector.
Check downspouts, splash blocks and drainage paths from the ground.
Look for wall stains under scuppers and gutter corners.
Trim trees and shrubs so branches stay well clear of the roof.
Do a final cool-weather attic peek before it gets too hot.
Plan any repairs to finish before June 15.

sections.body:
Since 2008, the National Weather Service has used fixed dates for Arizona's monsoon season: June 15 through September 30. Before that, the start was based on humidity readings, which meant the season began on a different day each year.

The fixed dates were meant to help people focus on storm safety for the whole period, rather than waiting for a technical start. It's a handy deadline for roof prep, too.

Spring calendars fill fast. To set up your inspection, call us at 602-548-3770, Monday to Friday, 7 am to 5 pm. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours. Next month: getting your roof and attic ready for summer heat.

faqs: How long does a roof inspection take?
It depends on the size, type and complexity of your roof. Many residential inspections take about an hour or two, including a look at the attic where it's accessible.
Do I need an inspection if my roof isn't leaking?

Yes, it's worth it. Many problems, like worn underlayment, cracked pipe boots or loose flashing, don't leak until a heavy storm hits. Spotting them early is usually easier and less costly than fixing a leak later.
What's the best month for a roof inspection in Phoenix?
March and April are ideal. The weather is mild, and there is enough time to schedule and complete repairs before monsoon season begins June 15.
Should I be home during the roof inspection?
It helps, though it isn't always required. Being there lets you point out concerns, open the attic access and hear the findings in person.
What happens after the inspection?
You'll learn what condition your roof is in and what, if anything, needs repair or replacement. If work is needed, you'll get an estimate so you can decide on next steps.
Can I do my own spring roof inspection?

You can do a useful first look from the ground with binoculars and from inside your home, checking ceilings and the attic in cool weather. A professional inspection covers what you can't safely see, like flashing, underlayment and tile condition up close. Please stay off the roof yourself.

headline: Let your attic breathe before the heat hits
title: Attic Ventilation Before Summer Heat | Integrity Roofing
desc: April roof tips: how attic ventilation helps your Phoenix roof handle summer heat, signs your attic runs too hot, and a safe DIY vent check.
h1: April 2027: Prepare your roof and attic for summer heat
lead: Triple-digit days are coming. Before they arrive, take a look at how your attic breathes, because ventilation affects your comfort, your energy bills and how long your roof lasts.
answer: Good attic ventilation lets hot air escape so heat doesn't build up under your roof, which protects roofing materials and eases the load on your air conditioner. In April, before temperatures climb, check that intake vents near the eaves and exhaust vents near the ridge are clear, that insulation isn't blocking them, and that the attic has no signs of trapped heat or moisture.

sections.h2: How heat affects your roof from below
sections.body:
Most people think about the sun beating down on the roof's surface. But heat also builds up from below, in the attic. When an attic can't vent hot air, temperatures there climb far above the outdoor air on summer afternoons. That trapped heat bakes the roof deck and underlayment from underneath and can shorten their life.

A hot attic also makes your home harder to cool. Heat radiates down through ceilings, and air conditioning ductwork running through the attic sits in that heat all day. Many homeowners notice upstairs rooms that never quite cool off. Ventilation won't solve every comfort issue, but it's an important piece.

A typical ventilated attic uses a balanced system. Intake vents, usually low on the roof near the eaves or in soffits, let cooler air in. Exhaust vents, near the ridge or high on the roof, let hot air out. As heat rises, it pulls fresh air through the attic in a steady flow.

Problems happen when that flow is blocked or out of balance. Insulation pushed against the eaves can cover intake vents. A vent damaged by a storm or clogged by a bird's nest can stop working. Adding vents without enough intake can pull conditioned air out of the house instead. A roofer can look at your setup during a roof inspection and tell you whether it's balanced.

sections.h2: DIY tip of the month: a spring vent check
sections.body:
April mornings are still cool enough for a short attic visit, so do it now rather than in June. From the attic hatch, with a flashlight, look toward the eaves. You should see gaps or baffles where outside air can enter. If insulation is packed tight against the roof deck there, the intake may be blocked.

Look for daylight at the vents, and check for nests, debris or droppings. From outside, use binoculars to look at roof vents for damage, missing screens or bird activity. Note anything you see and save your photos. Keep attic trips short, step only on joists or boards, and skip the attic entirely once days turn hot. Summer attics get dangerously hot.
Before the first 100-degree day:
bullets: Do a short, early-morning attic check for blocked intake vents.
Look for nests, droppings or debris near vent openings.
Use binoculars to check roof vents and screens from the ground.
Change your AC filter and have the system serviced if it's due.
Note upstairs rooms that run hot and mention them to your roofer.
Confirm bathroom and kitchen fans vent outside, not into the attic.
Finish any roof repairs before monsoon season begins June 15.

sections.body:
Building codes generally call for a minimum amount of attic ventilation based on attic floor area. A common baseline is 1 square foot of net vent area for every 150 square feet of attic, which can drop to 1 per 300 when intake and exhaust are balanced and other conditions are met.

Radiant barriers, a reflective layer often installed in hot-climate attics, work by reflecting radiant heat from the roof rather than absorbing it. They help most in sunny places like the Valley.

If your attic feels like an oven or your vents look damaged, call us at 602-548-3770, Monday to Friday, 7 am to 5 pm. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours. Next month: your final checklist before monsoon season.

faqs: How do I know if my attic is poorly ventilated?

Common signs include a very hot attic even in mild weather, upstairs rooms that are hard to cool, musty smells, or moisture and staining on the underside of the roof deck. A roofer can measure and assess your vent setup.
Can I add more vents to my roof myself?
We don't recommend it. Cutting into a roof creates leak risks and can throw ventilation out of balance. It also means working on the roof, which isn't safe for homeowners, especially on tile.
Does attic ventilation lower energy bills?
It can help, along with good insulation and sealed ductwork. Reducing attic heat means less heat radiating into your living space, which can ease the load on your air conditioner.
Is it safe to go into my attic in summer?
Generally, no. Attics in the Phoenix Valley can get dangerously hot by late morning in summer. Do attic checks in spring, fall or winter, and keep visits short.
What do soffit vents do?
Soffit vents sit under the roof overhang and let outside air into the attic. That air rises and exits through vents higher on the roof, carrying heat with it.

headline: Last call before monsoon
title: Final Pre-Monsoon Roof Prep Checklist | Integrity Roofing
desc: May roof tips for Phoenix homeowners: final pre-monsoon prep, from clearing drains and trimming trees to baseline photos, so your roof is ready by June 15.
h1: May 2027: Your final pre-monsoon roof prep
lead: Monsoon season starts June 15. May is your last comfortable month to finish repairs, clear the way for water and get your home ready for wind, dust and rain.
answer: In May, finish any roof repairs, clear gutters, downspouts and flat-roof drains, trim branches away from the roof, secure loose yard items, and take a full set of dated photos of your roof and home. Those baseline photos make it much easier to show what changed if a monsoon storm causes damage.

sections.body:
Monsoon storms can bring sudden high winds, blowing dust, heavy downpours and sometimes hail, often with little warning. A roof that is in good repair handles that well. A roof with a loose tile, a lifted shingle or a clogged drain is more likely to have trouble.

May is also getting hot. By the end of the month, outdoor work in the afternoon is uncomfortable and can be unsafe. Getting your prep done early in the month, in the mornings, is easier on you and gives roofers time to finish any repair work before June 15.

sections.h2: Wrap up repairs and clear the drains
sections.body:
If your spring inspection found problems, now is the time to finish them. Small issues like cracked tiles, worn pipe boots or loose flashing are exactly what monsoon wind and rain go looking for. Our repairs and maintenance page explains common fixes.

Next, think about water. Monsoon storms can drop a lot of rain in a short time. Gutters, downspouts and flat-roof scuppers need to be clear so water moves off the roof fast. On flat and foam roofs, clogged drains can lead to ponding, which adds weight and stresses the roof. Hire a pro for anything you can't reach safely from the ground.

sections.h2: DIY tip of the month: take baseline photos
sections.body:
This is one of the most useful things you can do before monsoon season, and it takes about 20 minutes. Walk around your home early in the morning and photograph each side of the house and each roof slope you can see from the ground. Use your phone's zoom or take pictures through binoculars for a closer look.

Include the gutters, the patio cover, the fascia and any skylights you can see. Inside, photograph ceilings in each room. Save everything in a folder labeled with the date. If a storm causes damage this summer, you'll have clear before-and-after images. As always, take every photo from the ground. Don't go up on the roof.
Finish these before June 15:
bullets: Complete any repairs from your spring inspection.
Clear gutters, downspouts and scuppers, or have them cleared.
Trim tree limbs that hang over or rub against the roof.
Secure or store patio furniture, umbrellas, trampolines and decor that can blow into the roof.
Take dated baseline photos of your roof, exterior and ceilings.
Find your homeowners insurance policy and know how to reach your insurer.
Save our number, 602-548-3770, in your phone.

sections.body:
The massive walls of dust that sometimes roll across the Valley in summer are called haboobs, a word borrowed from Arabic. They're created when outflow winds from a thunderstorm push dust ahead of the storm, and they can tower thousands of feet high.

Dust from these storms can settle into gutters and scuppers, mixing with rain into mud that clogs drains. That's one reason drainage checks matter so much during monsoon season.

If you'd like help wrapping up repairs before the storms, call us at 602-548-3770, Monday to Friday, 7 am to 5 pm. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours. Next month: monsoon season begins, and we'll cover how storms affect roofs and how to stay safe while watching them.

faqs: When does monsoon season start in Arizona?
The National Weather Service defines Arizona's monsoon season as June 15 through September 30. Storms don't always begin on day one, but it's smart to have your roof ready by then.
Why should I take photos of my roof before monsoon season?
Baseline photos show the condition of your roof and home before storms hit. If damage happens, before-and-after images help you, your roofer and your insurer understand what changed.
Do I need to trim trees near my roof?
Yes, if branches hang over or touch the roof. Monsoon winds can snap limbs onto the roof or rub branches against it. Hire a tree professional for large trees or high work.
How do I prepare a flat roof for monsoon season?
Keep drains and scuppers clear, make sure the coating is in good condition and watch for areas where water ponds. Have a roofer address any cracks, blisters or worn spots before storms arrive.
What yard items should I secure before monsoon storms?
Anything wind can lift: patio umbrellas, cushions, lightweight furniture, trampolines, trash cans and decorations. Strong gusts can throw these items into roofs, windows and cars.
Is it too late to schedule roof repairs in late May?

Not necessarily, but schedules can fill quickly before monsoon season. Call as early in the month as you can. If a repair can't be finished before June 15, ask your roofer about steps to reduce risk in the meantime.

headline: Monsoon season is here: know your storms
title: Monsoon Season Begins: Storm Watching | Integrity Roofing
desc: June roof tips: monsoon season starts June 15. Learn how dust, wind, rain and hail affect Phoenix roofs and how to watch storms safely from inside your home.
h1: June 2027: Monsoon season begins, and how to watch storms safely
lead: Monsoon season officially runs June 15 through September 30. This month we look at the storms themselves: what each one does to a roof, and how to keep an eye on your home safely while the weather rolls through.
answer: Monsoon storms bring four main threats to roofs: blowing dust, strong straight-line winds and microbursts, heavy downpours and occasional hail. During a storm, stay indoors, keep away from windows, and watch for warning signs from inside, such as drips, ceiling stains or loud impacts. Note the time of anything unusual so you can check it safely after the storm passes.

sections.h2: Four ways monsoon storms affect roofs
sections.body:
Dust. Dust storms arrive first, often ahead of the rain. Fine dust settles into gutters, valleys and scuppers. When rain follows, it can turn into mud that slows drainage.

Wind. Thunderstorm outflow winds and microbursts can produce sudden, powerful gusts. Wind can lift the edges of shingles, shift or crack tiles, peel back flashing and throw branches and patio items onto the roof.

Heavy rain. Monsoon rain often comes fast and hard. If drains are clogged, water can back up under roof edges or pond on flat roofs. Wind-driven rain can push water sideways into gaps that stay dry in a gentle shower.

Hail. Hail is less common in the Valley, but it does happen. It can crack tiles, bruise shingles and dent vents or flashing.

sections.h2: How to watch a storm safely
sections.body:
Monsoon storms are dramatic, and it's natural to want to watch. Do it from inside. Lightning can strike miles away from the heaviest rain, and flying debris is a real danger in strong winds. Stay away from windows and glass doors during the strongest gusts, and never go outside or onto a ladder to check on the roof mid-storm.

Instead, use your ears and eyes indoors. Loud cracks or thuds on the roof can mean debris or hail. Listen for water dripping in walls or ceilings. Walk through the house and look at ceilings, especially in rooms below valleys or where the roof meets a wall. If you see water, contain it with buckets and towels, and keep people away from sagging drywall.

sections.h2: DIY tip of the month: keep a storm log
sections.body:
A simple storm log is one of the best tools a homeowner can have during monsoon season. Keep a note on your phone. Each time a significant storm hits, write down the date, the approximate time, and what you noticed: high winds, hail, a loud impact, a drip, a flickering light.

Your notes help you remember which storm caused what, which is valuable if you ever need a repair or an insurance claim. They also help a roofer narrow down where to look. Add a quick photo from a window if it's safe. Everything stays indoors and on the ground, where it should.
For the first weeks of the season:
bullets: Start a storm log on your phone with dates, times and what you noticed.
Keep buckets, towels and a flashlight ready for surprise leaks.
Bring in or tie down patio items whenever a storm is forecast.
Watch storms from indoors and away from windows.
Listen for impacts and check ceilings during and right after heavy rain.
Wait for the storm to fully pass before stepping outside.
Keep your May baseline photos handy for comparison.

sections.body:
Before 2008, the start of Arizona's monsoon in Phoenix was tied to humidity. The season began after three straight days with an average dew point of 55 degrees or higher. The fixed June 15 start date replaced that rule to make safety messaging simpler.

The word monsoon comes from an Arabic word for season, and it refers to the seasonal shift in wind patterns that brings moisture into the Southwest, not to any single storm.

Stay safe and stay inside when storms roll through. If a storm leaves you with a leak or damage, call us at 602-548-3770, Monday to Friday, 7 am to 5 pm. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours. Next month: what to check after a storm passes.

faqs: What is a microburst?

A microburst is a powerful burst of sinking air from a thunderstorm that spreads out when it hits the ground. It can create very strong, damaging winds over a small area, which is why one street can see damage while the next one doesn't.
Can dust storms damage my roof?

Dust itself rarely causes direct damage, but it clogs gutters, valleys and drains. When rain follows, water can back up. The strong winds that come with dust storms can also loosen tiles and shingles.
Is it safe to check my roof during a monsoon storm?

No. Stay indoors until the storm has completely passed. Lightning, wind and flying debris make it dangerous to be outside, and wet roofs are extremely slippery. Check from inside and wait for calm, dry weather.
What should I do if my roof starts leaking during a storm?

Contain the water with buckets and towels, move belongings away, take photos and note the time. If water is near electrical fixtures, turn off power to that area at the breaker. Call a roofer once the storm passes.
Does hail happen in Phoenix?
It does, though it's less common than wind and heavy rain. When it falls, it can crack tiles and damage shingles, vents and flashing. Check for damage from the ground after a hailstorm.

headline: The storm passed. Now what?
title: After-Storm Roof Checks for Monsoon | Integrity Roofing
desc: July roof tips: a safe after-storm routine for Phoenix monsoon season, with what to check from the ground and inside your home after wind, rain or hail.
h1: July 2027: Your after-storm roof check, step by step
lead: July is often the heart of monsoon season. When a big storm moves through, a short, safe routine afterward helps you catch damage early, before the next storm makes it worse.
answer: After a monsoon storm passes and it's safe outside, walk around your home and look for debris, broken tile pieces, granules, displaced shingles, bent gutters and fallen branches. Then check ceilings and walls inside for new stains. Do all of it from the ground and inside your home, take photos, and call a roofer if you see anything unusual.

sections.body:
The first rule of after-storm checks is patience. Wait until the rain has stopped, the wind has died down and you no longer hear thunder. Monsoon storms can come in waves, so a lull doesn't always mean it's over.

When you do go out, watch for downed power lines and stay well away from them. Look out for broken glass, nails and sharp debris in the yard. And pick your timing: if the storm ended in the late afternoon heat, an early-morning walk the next day is often safer and more comfortable. In July, heat is a real hazard on its own.

sections.h2: What the ground can tell you
sections.body:
Your yard, patio and driveway are often the first place roof damage shows up. Look for pieces of broken tile, whole tiles, chunks of mortar, shingle pieces or loose flashing on the ground. A pile of granules at the bottom of a downspout after a storm can mean shingles took a beating, especially after hail.

Look up from several spots around the house. Use binoculars to scan for gaps in tile rows, lifted or missing shingles, displaced ridge caps, bent vents and branches resting on the roof. Check gutters for sagging or separated sections. On flat roofs, look for staining under scuppers that could mean water backed up.

sections.h2: DIY tip of the month: the inside sweep
sections.body:
After every big storm, do a quick sweep through your home. Start in rooms on the top floor or directly under the roof. Look at ceilings, especially near exterior walls, around skylights, light fixtures and vents. Check closets and the corners of rooms, where stains often show up first.

Look at window and door frames for water, and check the garage ceiling, which many people forget. Note anything new in your storm log with a photo. Skip the attic in July. Valley attics can get dangerously hot, even in the morning. If you suspect a leak above a ceiling, let a professional look.
After each major storm:
bullets: Wait until the storm has fully passed and avoid downed power lines.
Walk the yard for broken tiles, shingle pieces, flashing and branches.
Check downspout outlets for heavy granule buildup.
Scan each roof slope with binoculars from several angles.
Look for bent, sagging or separated gutters.
Do an inside sweep of ceilings, closets, windows and the garage.
Photograph anything new and add it to your storm log.

sections.body:
The National Weather Service classifies a thunderstorm as severe when it produces wind gusts of 58 mph or higher, hail 1 inch in diameter or larger, or a tornado. Monsoon storms in the Valley reach severe levels most often because of wind.

Damage from a single storm can be very patchy. One home can lose tiles while the house across the street is untouched, because the strongest gusts often affect a small area.

If your after-storm check turns up damage, see our damaged roof page and give us a call at 602-548-3770, Monday to Friday, 7 am to 5 pm. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours. Next month: how to document storm damage the right way.

faqs: How soon after a storm should I check my roof?
As soon as it's safe, ideally the same day or early the next morning. Catching damage quickly helps prevent a second storm from turning a small problem into a leak.
What does it mean if I find tile pieces in my yard?
It usually means one or more tiles cracked or broke, possibly from wind or impact. Even a small missing piece can expose the underlayment, so it's worth having a roofer take a look.
Can I tell if my roof has hail damage from the ground?
Sometimes. Look for granules at downspouts, dents in metal vents or gutters, and cracked tiles. Many hail marks are only visible up close, so a professional inspection is the safest way to know.
Should I go into the attic to look for leaks in July?
We don't recommend it. Attics in the Phoenix Valley can reach dangerous temperatures in summer. Check ceilings from inside your home and let a roofer handle anything above them.
What if I don't see any damage but I'm still worried?

Some damage, like loosened flashing or underlayment tears, isn't visible from the ground. If a storm was especially strong, or you notice anything odd later, a roof inspection can give you peace of mind.

headline: Document it like a pro
title: How to Document Monsoon Roof Damage | Integrity Roofing
desc: August roof tips: how to document monsoon roof damage with photos, notes and records, so you're ready to work with a roofer and your insurance company.
h1: August 2027: How to document monsoon roof damage
lead: When a storm damages your roof, good records make everything easier. This month we cover how to document damage clearly, safely and in a way that helps your roofer and your insurer.
answer: To document monsoon roof damage, take dated photos and videos from the ground and inside your home, write down the storm date and what you observed, keep damaged pieces you find in the yard, and save every receipt and report. Compare against your pre-season photos. Contact your insurance company promptly and review your policy for its deadlines.

sections.body:
Storm damage can be stressful. Clear records cut down on back-and-forth and help everyone see the same picture. A roofer can use your notes and photos to narrow down where to look. If you file an insurance claim, documentation helps show when the damage happened and how it relates to a specific storm.

Good records also protect you over time. Damage that seems minor in August can show up as a leak during winter rain. If you have dated photos and notes from the storm, you have a clear history of what happened and when.

Start with the big picture, then move to the details. Photograph each side of the house from the yard, then zoom in on damage you can see from the ground, such as missing or broken tiles, lifted shingles, bent gutters or debris on the roof. Short videos panning across the roof or the yard can add helpful context.

Inside, photograph every stain, drip and damaged item, with something nearby for scale. Collect broken tile pieces or shingles that landed in the yard and set them aside. Write down the storm date, the time, what you heard or saw, and any steps you took, like moving furniture or placing buckets. Your storm log and May baseline photos are a big help here.

Every policy is different, so read yours and call your insurer with questions. Many policies have time limits for reporting damage, and some require you to take reasonable steps to prevent further damage. Keep notes on every conversation, including the date and the person you spoke with.

A roofer can inspect the roof up close and explain what they find, which can be helpful when you talk with an adjuster. You can learn more about storm repairs on our damaged roof page.

sections.h2: DIY tip of the month: build a storm folder
sections.body:
Create one folder, on your phone, computer or in a paper file, just for this monsoon season. Inside, keep subfolders for baseline photos, storm photos, your storm log, insurance notes and receipts. Name photos or folders with the date so they stay in order.

Back everything up to a second place, like cloud storage. Take every photo from the ground, a window or inside the house. Please don't climb on the roof to get a better shot. Broken tiles make roofs even more hazardous, and August heat makes roof surfaces dangerous to touch. A roofer can take close-up photos during an inspection.
When a storm causes damage:
bullets: Photograph the outside from the ground, wide and close-up.
Photograph inside damage, with a common object for scale.
Save broken roof pieces you find in the yard.
Write down the storm date, time and what you observed.
Review your policy and contact your insurer promptly.
Keep receipts for buckets, tarps, cleanup or temporary repairs.
Back up all records in a second location.

sections.body:
The National Weather Service safety saying is short and memorable: when thunder roars, go indoors. If you can hear thunder, you're close enough to be struck by lightning, even if the rain hasn't reached you yet.

Most smartphone photos automatically record the date and time they were taken, which can be helpful when you need to show when damage occurred. Keeping the original files, not just edited copies, preserves that information.

If you need an up-close look at storm damage, call us at 602-548-3770, Monday to Friday, 7 am to 5 pm. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours. Next month: the end-of-season inspection.

faqs: How soon should I report storm damage to my insurer?
As soon as you reasonably can. Many policies have reporting time limits, and waiting can make it harder to connect damage to a specific storm. Check your policy or call your insurer to confirm.
Should I clean up debris before taking photos?
Take photos first, then clean up. Pictures of debris where it landed help show what happened. Set aside pieces of broken tile or shingle in case someone needs to see them.
Can a roofer help with documentation?

Yes. A roofer can inspect the roof up close, take photos of damage you can't see from the ground and explain what they find. That information can be useful when you speak with your insurance adjuster.
What if damage shows up months after a storm?

Contact your insurer and a roofer as soon as you notice it. Your storm log and dated photos can help show when the damage likely occurred. Policies differ, so ask your insurer how they handle late-discovered damage.
Should I make temporary repairs myself?
Indoors, it's fine to contain water and protect belongings. Leave anything on the roof, including tarps, to a professional. Keep receipts for any supplies you buy for temporary protection.

headline: Close out monsoon season right
title: End-of-Monsoon Roof Inspection Guide | Integrity Roofing
desc: September roof tips: monsoon season ends September 30. Why an end-of-season roof inspection matters, what it covers, and how to prepare your roof for fall.
lead: Monsoon season ends September 30. Before you put storm season out of your mind, take one more step: an end-of-season inspection to catch any damage the summer left behind.
answer: Schedule an end-of-season roof inspection in late September or October to catch hidden damage from monsoon wind, rain and heat before winter rains arrive. Bring your storm log and photos, ask about tiles, flashing, underlayment, coatings and drainage, and get repairs done during fall's mild weather.

sections.body:
Over a full monsoon season, your roof may face dozens of storms. Some damage is obvious, like a missing tile. But a lot of storm damage is subtle. Wind can lift a tile just enough to break a seal, loosen flashing without pulling it off, or tear underlayment that no one can see from the ground. Summer heat adds wear on top of that.

Many of these problems won't leak right away. They wait for the long, steady rains of winter. An end-of-season inspection finds them while the weather is about to turn mild, which is the easiest time to make repairs.

sections.h2: What an end-of-season inspection looks at
sections.body:
A post-monsoon roof inspection focuses on what storms and heat tend to affect. That includes cracked, slipped or missing tiles, lifted or creased shingles, displaced ridge and hip caps, flashing around walls and chimneys, pipe boots and vents, and valleys where debris collects.

On flat and foam roofs, the inspector looks at the coating for wear, blisters or punctures from debris, and checks drains and scuppers for buildup from dust and leaves. Where it's accessible and safe, a look in the attic can reveal stains or damp spots from summer storms. You should come away with a clear list of what's fine and what needs attention.

sections.h2: DIY tip of the month: compare your photos
sections.body:
Pull up the baseline photos you took in May and your storm photos from the summer. Then, on a cooler morning, take a new set from the same spots around your home. Put them side by side.

Look for changes: tiles that have shifted, gaps that weren't there before, gutters that sag, new stains on walls or ceilings. Mark anything that looks different and bring the comparison to your inspection. Do all of this from the ground and inside your home. Late September can still bring triple-digit heat, so keep outdoor time short and stay off the roof.
To wrap up monsoon season:
bullets: Take a fresh set of photos from the same spots as your May baseline.
Compare before-and-after photos for any changes.
Gather your storm log, photos and insurance notes.
Schedule an end-of-season roof inspection.
Clear dust and debris from gutters, downspouts and scuppers.
Check ceilings and closets one more time for stains.
Plan any repairs for October or November, before winter rains.

sections.body:
Phoenix averages only about 7 inches of rain a year, and a meaningful share of it falls during the summer monsoon. The rest comes mostly from winter storms, which is why the Valley's roof calendar really has two wet seasons to plan around.

Monsoon rainfall can vary hugely from place to place. One neighborhood may get a soaking while another a few miles away stays dry, so your own observations matter more than citywide totals.

Thanks for reading The Integrity Roofing Monthly through another storm season. To set up your end-of-season inspection, call us at 602-548-3770, Monday to Friday, 7 am to 5 pm. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours. Next month: a fall roof check as the heat finally breaks.

faqs: When does monsoon season end in Arizona?
Monsoon season officially ends September 30. Storms can taper off earlier or, occasionally, linger, but the official dates are June 15 through September 30.
Do I need an inspection if I didn't notice any storm damage?
It's still a good idea, especially after an active season. Wind and heat can cause damage that isn't visible from the ground and may not leak until winter rains arrive.
What should I bring to my end-of-season inspection?
Bring your storm log, before-and-after photos, notes on any leaks or concerns, and insurance information if you've filed a claim. That helps the inspector focus on the right areas.
Is it too late to file an insurance claim for a July storm?
It depends on your policy. Many have reporting time limits, so contact your insurer as soon as possible and share your dated photos and notes.
When should I schedule repairs after the inspection?
October and November are ideal. The weather is mild, and repairs finished in fall prepare your roof for winter storms that usually start in December.
What kind of damage do monsoon storms leave that I can't see?

Common hidden damage includes tiles that shifted just enough to let water under them, loosened flashing, torn or exposed underlayment, cracked pipe boots, and small punctures in flat-roof coatings from blowing debris. None of these may leak right away, but winter rain often finds them. An up-close inspection is the best way to catch them.
